cards.title: Complements: the platform's demand engine
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Two products are complements if a drop in the price of one pushes out the demand curve for the other.
cards.why: The one-line economics behind the whole platform playbook: open the platform, let outsiders build complements, watch demand for your product rise.
cards.uw: When you're deciding whether to open up or lock down.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 7: Paying Complements, and Other Smart Strategies

cards.title: The crowd is the opposite of the core
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: The crowd is, in many ways, the opposite of the core: it’s huge, diverse, largely uncontrollable, and often messy.
cards.why: The third rebalance stated as a contrast: the core is built, the crowd is found — huge, diverse, uncontrollable, and increasingly more powerful than what's inside.
cards.uw: When you're weighing an internal team against the world outside it.

cards.title: The crowd beats the credentialed core, repeatedly
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Over and over again, the recognized experts of the core see their performance beaten by uncredentialed and conventionally inexperienced members of the crowd.
cards.why: The empirical claim of the crowd section: it's not a theory about openness, it's a track record of outsiders beating insiders.
cards.uw: When the experts say only experts can solve it.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 11: Why the Expert You Know Is Not the Expert You Need

cards.title: Why companies survive: incomplete contracting
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Companies and other nonmarket organizations are needed to deal with the problem of incomplete contracting—the fact that contracts cannot realistically specify all possible contingencies in the messy real world.
cards.why: The authors' answer to their own provocative chapter title: the crowd can't replace companies because contracts can't cover reality — someone has to hold the residual right to decide.
cards.uw: When decentralization hype says companies are finished.

cards.title: Ask what we want to do with technology
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: So we should ask not “What will technology do to us?” but rather “What do we want to do with technology?”
cards.why: The book's closing reversal: technology is a tool, not a fate — the question was never what it does to us, but what we choose to do with it.
cards.uw: When the conversation turns fatalist about AI, platforms, or crowds.
cards.source_locator: Conclusion: Economies and Societies Beyond Computation

cards.title: Things get weird in the second half of the chessboard
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: In other words, things get weird in the second half of the chessboard. And like the emperor, most of us have trouble keeping up.
cards.why: The book's master metaphor: exponential growth stays inside human intuition for the first 32 doublings, then leaves it behind entirely — which is where digital technology now lives.
cards.uw: When someone projects a technology trend in a straight line.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Moore's Law and the Second Half of the Chessboard

cards.title: American business entered the second half in 2006
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: U.S. businesses entered the second half of the chessboard when it comes to the use of digital gear. That was in 2006.
cards.why: Pins the metaphor to a date: counting doublings of corporate IT investment since 1958, the disorientation regime began nearly a decade before the book was written — it isn't coming, it's here.
cards.uw: When dating when the AI economy actually began.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Moore's Law and the Second Half of the Chessboard

cards.title: Bounty: the best economic news in the world today
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Bounty is the increase in volume, variety, and quality and the decrease in cost of the many offerings brought on by modern technological progress. It’s the best economic news in the world today.
cards.why: The optimistic half of the book's frame, defined with precision: more stuff, better stuff, cheaper stuff — the part of the story the doomers leave out.
cards.uw: When the AI debate goes all-doom.

cards.title: Spread: ever-bigger differences in economic success
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Spread, however, is not so great; it’s ever-bigger differences among people in economic success—in wealth, income, mobility, and other important measures.
cards.why: The pessimistic half, defined with matching precision: the same technology that multiplies the bounty distributes it unevenly — and the spread is accelerating too.
cards.uw: When someone cites growth statistics that hide distribution.

cards.title: The driver is exponential, digital, and combinatorial
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Instead, the main driver is exponential, digital, and combinatorial change in the technology that undergirds our economic system.
cards.why: The authors' causal claim, ruling out the usual suspects: tax policy, trade, and Wall Street aren't the primary drivers of inequality — the technology itself is.
cards.uw: When hunting the root cause of wage stagnation.

cards.title: The Great Decoupling
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: While these two key economic statistics tracked each other for most of the postwar period, they became decoupled in the late 1990s. Productivity continued its upward path as employment sagged.
cards.why: The chart that broke the postwar deal: productivity at record highs while employment and median income flatline — growth no longer lifts all boats automatically.
cards.uw: When someone says economic growth lifts all boats.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 11: Implications of the Bounty and the Spread

cards.title: We know more than we can tell
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: “We know more than we can tell.”
cards.why: Polanyi's line was the great defense of human work — tacit knowledge that can't be boiled down to rules can't be computerized. The book's twist: machines learned pattern recognition anyway, and the defense is collapsing task by task.
cards.uw: When someone claims their job is safe because it needs 'human judgment.'
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Skills of the New Machines

cards.title: Weak human plus machine plus better process
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Weak human + machine + better process was superior to a strong computer alone and, more remarkably, superior to a strong human + machine + inferior process.
cards.why: Freestyle chess proved the formula: process beats both raw talent and raw compute. The amateurs with three laptops beat grandmasters with supercomputers — how you combine with the machine matters more than either side alone.
cards.uw: When designing how your team actually uses AI tools.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 12: Learning to Race with Machines

cards.title: Race with machines, not against them
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: people still have a great deal to offer the game of chess at its highest levels once they’re allowed to race with machines, instead of purely against them.
cards.why: The book's answer to automation anxiety: the winning move is partnership, not competition. Humans contribute strategic guidance; machines contribute tactical acuity — and the combination beats both.
cards.uw: When the automation debate turns zero-sum.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 12: Learning to Race with Machines

cards.title: Close enough to zero to create strange economics
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: While the marginal costs of digital goods do not quite approach zero, they are close enough to create some pretty strange economics.
cards.why: Near-zero marginal cost is the engine under winner-take-all: one producer with a website can serve billions, so capacity constraints — the thing that used to spread markets around — become irrelevant.
cards.uw: When explaining why digital markets concentrate into monopolies.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 10: The Biggest Winners: Stars and Superstars

cards.title: Free news that shrinks GDP
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: replacing a paid newspaper with an equivalent free news service would decrease GDP even though it increased consumer surplus.
cards.why: The measurement crisis in one sentence: GDP counts paid transactions, not wellbeing, so the digital bounty — free, better, everywhere — is invisible to the scoreboard we run the economy on.
cards.uw: When GDP says the economy is fine but life feels better than the numbers.

cards.title: Possibilities do not merely add up; they multiply
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Possibilities do not merely add up; they multiply.
cards.why: Romer's recombinant engine, adopted as the book's theory of innovation: digital networks let ideas combine and recombine without limit, so the innovation pool compounds instead of depleting.
cards.uw: When someone argues we've run out of big ideas.

cards.title: Give people money
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Many of them have proposed the same simple solution: give people money.
cards.why: The authors' long-term answer to spread: basic income — an equal yearly payment, no means testing — with a lineage from Thomas Paine to MLK, as the way to share the bounty when labor alone can't.
cards.uw: When the conversation turns to what happens if the jobs don't come back.

cards.title: The future depends on the choices we make
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Technology creates possibilities and potential, but ultimately, the future we get will depend on the choices we make.
cards.why: The closing rejection of technological determinism: the second machine age hands us vastly more power to change the world, and with it the responsibility to choose what kind of world — bounty shared or disaster.
cards.uw: When the AI future is framed as inevitable.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: A strategy is a concept; a TradeBook is a manual
cards.steal: There is a fundamental difference between a strategy and a TradeBook. A strategy outlines the overall concept—what to look for in a particular type of trade and how that trade generally works. A TradeBook, however, is much more practical, more like a manual.
cards.why: The book's spine sentence: a strategy only says what to look for, a TradeBook scripts selection, identification, planning, entries, exits, stops, position sizing, management, and psychology.
cards.uw: When someone pitches a 'strategy' with no rules for entries, exits, or review.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: The edge is the combination, not one piece
cards.steal: The edge in trading doesn’t come from any one of these pieces on their own. It comes from combining them into a system that works for you. That’s what a TradeBook helps you build—a personalized, complete, and practical trading guide based on your tools, your mindset, and your strategy.
cards.why: Technology, strategy, and psychology each fail alone; the TradeBook is the overlap where all three meet, and that overlap is the only durable edge.
cards.uw: When a trader keeps buying better tools instead of building a system.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Gamification traded against the retail trader
cards.steal: A November 2024 study shed light on this trend, analyzing 142 gamification features in the mobile trading apps of 17 major U.S. brokers. The research found that while these features successfully increased retail trading activity and income for brokers and market makers, they often led to lower returns and higher volatility for the retail traders themselves.
cards.why: The technology chapter's warning: the tools were built to increase broker income, and they work — by making you trade more and win less.
cards.uw: When a flashy app makes trading feel like a game and you trade more than planned.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Consistent hours, consistent results
cards.steal: The consistency of your trading hours has a direct impact on the consistency of your results.
cards.why: A one-line case for routine as infrastructure: concentrated volatility at defined hours lets a retail trader be sharp; 24/7 markets invite 24/7 bleed.
cards.uw: When your trading day has no edges and neither do your results.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Sitting out is a skill
cards.steal: Recognizing when not to trade is as valuable as knowing when to take a position.
cards.why: Most price action is choppy with no clear winner; the discipline to wait for a readable signal is priced like an entry skill.
cards.uw: When you feel the pull to trade an ambiguous tape.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Understanding Price Action and Developing Well-Defined Strategies

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Your edge is a TradeBook, codified and identifiable
cards.steal: Bear Bull Traders calls your edge in the markets your “TradeBooks”, and we define your edge as a specific market opportunity codified in a specific TradeBook, which is repeatedly identifiable, and provides you with a positive expected value in profit, over time, when executed with discipline.
cards.why: The formal definition: an edge is not a feeling about a setup, it is an opportunity written down, repeatedly recognizable, and positive-expectancy — the casino model of trading.
cards.uw: When asked to name your edge and you can only describe vibes.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: The TradeBook answers: should I take this trade?
cards.steal: If you cannot put the trade opportunity into any of your TradeBooks, it means you should not take that trade. And this is the most important purpose of your TradeBooks. They help you answer the question: Should I take the trade or not?
cards.why: The TradeBook's gatekeeping function: it converts 'this looks good' into a binary fit-or-skip decision, which is where most retail losses begin.
cards.uw: When a tempting setup does not quite fit your plan but you want it anyway.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Success is not being right most of the time
cards.steal: This highlights a vital aspect of trading: success is not about being right most of the time. Instead, it is about ensuring that your winning trades are large enough to outweigh your losses.
cards.why: Seven years of ORB research: stopped out 75% of the time, profitable on 25%, and still beating the market — expectancy, not win rate, is the scoreboard.
cards.uw: When a low win rate tempts you to abandon a working system.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Drawdowns are asymmetric: 50% down needs 100% to recover
cards.steal: A 50% loss means you will need to double your account (100%) just to get back to even.
cards.why: Losses compound against you, which is why the stop loss is the foundation of the whole system: capital protection is the edge beneath the edge.
cards.uw: When sizing up a trade, run the recovery math first.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Not home runs; the long game
cards.steal: This calculation demonstrates why protecting your capital and maintaining consistent, small gains are key to long-term success. It is not about hitting home runs; it is about playing the long game.
cards.why: 0.5% a day compounded grows an account nearly 20-fold in three years — the math case for boring consistency over spectacular trades.
cards.uw: When impatience pushes you toward the big swing instead of the small edge.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Psychology means executing the TradeBook exactly as intended
cards.steal: So, from here on in, when I talk about trading psychology, I am talking about the mindset and emotional control that enables you to execute your TradeBooks, exactly as intended, every time you trade.
cards.why: Sheehy-Kelly de-fogs trading psychology: it is not vibes or affirmations, it is the measurable ability to execute the book you wrote — the mental edge.
cards.uw: When psychology talk drifts into mysticism instead of execution discipline.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 5: Building a Trading Psychology Edge

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Execute the TradeBook above the PNL
cards.steal: Prioritize the successful execution of your TradeBooks above your PNL.
cards.why: The counterintuitive core of the psychology chapter: over-focusing on the money is what produces the rule-breaking that loses the money — measure the process instead.
cards.uw: When a green day of sloppy trading feels like success, or a disciplined red day feels like failure.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 5: Building a Trading Psychology Edge

cards.title: Civil-Military Relations and Militarization in El Salvador
cards.book: Civil-Military Relations and Militarization in El Salvador — Stephen D. Rittermann
cards.steal: Under FMLN president Mauricio Funes (2009-2014), informal civil-military relations produced a largely undemocratic domestic-security response — troops in the streets — and a rising trend of militarization; the 1992 Chapultepec Peace Accords demobilized the old war but never reintegrated former combatants or rebuilt the economy, leaving transnational gangs and the drug trade as democratic El Salvador's dominant security challenge.
cards.why: It shows the mechanism by which a post-war democracy quietly remilitarizes — when the civilian police can't hold and the army fills the streets, the civil-military bargain reverts without a coup.
cards.uw: Informal civil-military relations produce undemocratic security policy — the institution you use for the emergency becomes the institution that defines normal.

cards.title: Providing orbit information with predetermined bounded accuracy
cards.book: Providing orbit information with predetermined bounded accuracy — Vitali Braun
cards.steal: Instead of handing satellite operators raw time-tagged position tables (forcing every operator to extrapolate on his own), orbit data can be delivered as Chebyshev polynomial coefficients that directly encode the state vector and covariance matrix over a time span — derived from a reference orbit by a least-squares fit with a modified geopotential, producing orbit information of predetermined, bounded accuracy for any Earth orbit.
cards.why: Collision-avoidance warnings are only as good as the orbit data every party shares — this is the plumbing that lets thousands of operators agree on where every object is, at the accuracy each is entitled to, without each re-running the math.
cards.uw: Don't ship raw data and make every consumer do the hard math — ship the answer at the accuracy each consumer is entitled to.

cards.title: China's role in counter-piracy operations
cards.book: China's role in counter-piracy operations — Ann K. Patterson
cards.steal: China's counter-piracy deployments in the Gulf of Aden and Southeast Asia were never just about pirates — they were a stepping-stone for a much larger maritime strategy. Comparing the two regions, the thesis finds some truth in all three explanations (meeting rivals' challenges and establishing geopolitical position; safeguarding economic interests; cooperating as a good global citizen) — and the deployments left China with a better-trained, more capable, more versatile navy, expanded economic reach, and tactics learned through cooperation with other navies.
cards.why: It names the mechanism of naval expansion through ostensibly benign missions — counter-piracy as the cover story under which a blue-water navy gets built, exercised, and normalized.
cards.uw: A mission's stated purpose and its strategic function can both be true at once — ask what the deployment builds, not just what it fights.

cards.title: Open Receptacles: Imagination in Continental and Process Thought, and the Opening of Religious Pluralism
cards.book: Open Receptacles: Imagination in Continental and Process Thought, and the Opening of Religious Pluralism — Rafael Reyes III
cards.steal: Religious pluralism looks impossible when reason is restricted to logic alone — logic forces a single outcome and hierarchizes or excludes faiths that don't fit its criteria; but with imagination (logic plus aesthetics, via Whitehead's immanence and creativity) admitted as a method, pluralism becomes integral to truth formation, religious experience, and a deeper understanding of the Divine.
cards.why: A transferable move — when a method can only produce one winner, the problem is the method's ontology, not the question; adding imagination (aesthetics) back into reasoning changes what counts as true.
cards.uw: If your method admits only one right answer, it will manufacture losers — expand the method before you condemn the question.

cards.title: Raízes Sofísticas – Sobre a escrita como phármakon para a fala (ou Da tradição gorgiana até Alcidamante de Eleia)
cards.book: Raízes Sofísticas – Sobre a escrita como phármakon para a fala (ou Da tradição gorgiana até Alcidamante de Eleia) — Lucio Lauro Barrozo Massafferri Salles
cards.steal: Gorgias treated language as a drug (phármakon) acting on the psyche, and his disciple Alcidamas pushed the argument further: writing is a subsidiary, inferior mode of language compared to live speech — the improvising speaker reads the room and rides its desires, while the writer, locked into a text prepared in advance, mistimes the moment, because no human foresight can predict exactly how an audience's mind will move.
cards.why: The oldest argument for why live performance beats the script — a 2,400-year-old account of why pre-written communication fails in any medium that rewards reading the room.
cards.uw: A fixed script can't read the room — the power of live speech is adaptation to the moment, which no amount of preparation fully simulates.

cards.title: The Wolfe Detective Game
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: Your goal isn't to "understand the story." Your goal is to figure out what Severian is accidentally telling you. And you don't get to assume he's telling the truth. Keep three columns as you read. WHAT HAPPENED: what Severian explicitly says happened. WHAT I THINK HAPPENED: your interpretation. WHAT'S WEIRD: anything that doesn't quite fit. Don't solve it immediately. That's the fun. Wolfe hid the instructions inside the book itself: the brown book says "everything, whatever happens, has three meanings. The first is its practical meaning, what the book calls, 'the thing the plowman sees.'"
cards.why: The narrator warns you in sentence one that certainty is off the table, then the brown book hands you the method: three meanings per thing, three columns per scene. The game isn't fan theory — it's the intended interface. Severian never lies about what he saw; he just never does the arithmetic. That's your job.
cards.uw: Use when reading any narrator who insists on his own honesty.

cards.title: The first sentence is a hedge
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "It is possible I already had some presentiment of my future." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** He's opening his confession. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** The man who will later swear he never forgets anything opens his life's account with "it is possible." He isn't sure about his own foreshadowing.
cards.why: Wolfe tells you in sentence one that certainty is off the table, then spends four books daring you to forget he said so. Every confident claim after this sentence has to survive it.
cards.uw: Use when a narrator's confidence and his evidence don't match.

cards.title: The man who never forgets can't get to bed
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "How I reached my bed I have no notion... I (who never forget anything, who, if I may for once confess the truth, though I seem to boast, do not truly understand what others mean when they say forget, for it seems to me that all experience becomes a part of my being) only slept and was carried there." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** He got drunk and blacked out. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** He asserts perfect memory inside a sentence confessing a gap in it. Both claims can't be true, and he notices neither.
cards.why: This is the whole game in one paragraph — the contradiction isn't hidden, it's decorated. Once you see him do it here, you'll catch him doing it everywhere.
cards.uw: Use when someone's boast and their admission arrive in the same breath.

cards.title: Perhaps, 589 times
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "Perhaps she was a servant from some remote part of the Citadel. Perhaps she was a resident of the city, who for gain or because of some old connection with our guild consented to play the part; I do not know." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** He's guessing. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** I counted: the man with total recall says "perhaps" 589 times across the four books. Perfect memory shouldn't need hedging — unless the hedging IS the memory, marking every spot where he knows more than he'll say or less than he claims.
cards.why: Wolfe's favorite dodge word is a tell. Each "perhaps" is a little flag planted on a fact Severian won't commit to. Count the hedges and you map his evasions.
cards.uw: Use when counting someone's hedges tells you more than their claims.

cards.title: The coin knows his hiding place
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** Vodalus presses a gold chrisos into his palm at a grave robbery. Alone the next day: "This one bore what I at first thought was a woman's face — a woman crowned, neither young nor old, but silent and perfect in the citrine metal. At last I turned my treasure over, and then indeed I caught my breath; stamped on the reverse was just such a flying ship as I had seen in the arms above the door of my secret mausoleum." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** The coin is a rebel token. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** How does a rebel leader's pocket change bear the arms over the door of a boy's secret hiding place? Severian writes "it seemed beyond explanation" and moves on. Don't you move on.
cards.why: The "beyond explanation" moments are the load-bearing ones — Wolfe marks his mysteries by having Severian refuse to look at them. The shrug is the clue.
cards.uw: Use when a coincidence gets one sentence and a shrug.

cards.title: He invents a word and everyone nods
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "'Severian. I am a torturer. Or rather, I am an apprentice of the torturers, Liege. Of the Order of the Seekers for Truth and Penitence.' I drew a deep breath. 'I am a Vodalarius. One of the thousands of Vodalarii of whose existence you are unaware.' It was a term I had scarcely heard." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** He pledged himself to Vodalus. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** He coins "Vodalarius" on the spot — "a term I had scarcely heard" — and the great rebel accepts it without blinking. Either the word is real and Severian's lying about inventing it, or it's fake and Vodalus is playing along. Both are interesting.
cards.why: Severian's lies work because he tells them to people who need them to be true — watch who never checks. The detective question is rarely "is he lying"; it's "who profits from not noticing."
cards.uw: Use when a made-up word sails through unchallenged.

cards.title: How old is Dorcas? Wrong question.
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "How old would you say Dorcas is? Eighteen? Nineteen, perhaps?" She is found by the water, young and golden-haired, mud caking in her hair. Much later she walks home alone: "she had lived forty years ago or more though it had now fallen into decay." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** She's a young woman Severian rescued. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** You don't go home to a house you lived in "forty years ago or more" when you're nineteen. Severian reports both facts and connects neither.
cards.why: The Dorcas case teaches the game's golden rule: Severian never lies about what he saw — he just never does the arithmetic. The facts are all on the page; the conclusion is your move.
cards.uw: Use when two true facts in the same story can't both be true.

cards.title: 'I am Thecla, if you want me to be'
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** With a fellow apprentice's silver he takes a girl upstairs; halfway through undressing her he stops cold: "There was nothing of Thecla about her. All that had been a chance resemblance, some gestures, a similarity in dress." He demands, "You are not the Chatelaine Thecla. What am I doing here with you?" She answers: "I am Thecla. If you want me to be." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** A brothel transaction. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** His hands picked the girl who looked like Thecla; his mouth claims it was chance. Which is telling the truth — the hands or the mouth? And why is he already haunted by a prisoner of his own guild he claims to barely know?
cards.why: The first Thecla-doubling happens while she is still alive, not after the tragedy — the haunting starts before the catastrophe. Wolfe shows you the obsession first and the disaster later. The detective reads backwards.
cards.uw: Use when someone's actions name the want their words won't.

cards.title: Infinite Severians
cards.book: The Book of the New Sun — Gene Wolfe
cards.steal: **WHAT HAPPENED:** "At one place in the Hall of Meaning there are two mirrors... anyone who walks down the Hall of Meaning sees himself infinitely multiplied there. Each mirror reflects the images in its twin." **WHAT I THINK HAPPENED:** Palace decoration. **WHAT'S WEIRD:** Wolfe puts a machine for generating infinite Severians in the hall called Meaning. Every reflection claims to be the real one. Sound like any narrator you know?
cards.why: The mirrors are the book's thesis rendered as furniture: the boy, the torturer, the Autarch, the writer — each reflects the others, and none will tell you which one is holding the pen. The three-column game exists because there are infinite columns.
cards.uw: Use when the story's furniture is the story's argument.

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: All violence as a means is either law-making or law-preserving
cards.steal: All violence as a means is either law-making or law-preserving. If it lays claim to neither of these predicates, it forfeits all validity.
cards.why: The essay's master distinction: every violence the state deploys is either founding a legal order or defending one — there is no third, neutral kind.
cards.uw: Classifying any state use of force, from airstrikes to arrests.

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: Lawmaking is power making
cards.steal: Lawmaking is power making, and, to that extent, an immediate manifestation of violence. Justice is the principle of all divine end making, power the principle of all mythical lawmaking.
cards.why: Founding a legal order is itself an act of violence — justice and power are different principles, and law is built on the second while claiming the first.
cards.uw: Someone treats the law as neutral ground rather than a settlement imposed by force.

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: The police suspend the distinction
cards.steal: The police intervene "for security reasons" in countless cases where no clear legal situation exists, when they are not merely permitted by law to act but when the legal order is not directly threatened.
cards.why: The police are the zone where law-making and law-preserving blur into one body — acting where law cannot reach, which is why every emergency eventually lives there permanently.
cards.uw: "For security reasons" appears as the justification.

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: Mythic violence vs divine violence
cards.steal: If mythical violence is lawmaking, divine violence is law-destroying; if the former sets boundaries, the latter boundlessly destroys them; if mythical violence brings at once guilt and retribution, divine power only expiates; if the former threatens, the latter strikes; if the former is bloody the latter is lethal without spilling blood.
cards.why: Benjamin's exit from the circle: a violence that neither founds nor preserves law but annihilates it — the essay's answer to a legal order that feeds on its own exceptions.
cards.uw: A rupture fits neither revolution (new law) nor reform (same law).

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: The state fears violence for its mere existence outside the law
cards.steal: The interest of the law in a monopoly of violence vis-a-vis individuals is explained not by the intention of preserving legal ends but, rather, by the intention of preserving the law itself; that violence, when not in the hands of the law, threatens it not by the ends that it may pursue but by its mere existence outside the law.
cards.why: The monopoly on force isn't about public safety — it's about the law's self-preservation. Rival violence is threatening simply by existing outside the state's hands.
cards.uw: A crackdown looks wildly disproportionate to the actual threat.

cards.book: Critique of Violence — Walter Benjamin
cards.title: 'Thou shalt not kill' is a guideline, not a criterion
cards.steal: "Thou shalt not kill" is not a criterion for judgement. It is a guideline for the actions of persons or communities who have to wrestle with it in solitude and, in exceptional cases, to take on themselves the responsibility of ignoring it.
cards.why: Even the absolute commandment leaves the exception to solitary responsibility — no law can decide in advance when it may be suspended, which is exactly where sovereign power lives.
cards.uw: The exception is invoked and someone claims the law already settled it.

cards.title: The experiment becomes the authority
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Mike begins as the ultimate outsider learning humanity from scratch, and ends as the man with the explanation. The dangerous transformation is not that he learns: it is that everyone else's willingness to project meaning onto him manufactures his authority before he has earned it.
cards.why: Charismatic authority is a demand-side phenomenon. The outsider does not seize the microphone; the audience hands it to him because they are desperate for someone to explain reality to them. Test every guru story against this: who needed the explanation first?
cards.uw: Someone with exotic credentials, foreign, technical, or outsider, is being handed interpretive authority they have not demonstrated.
cards.source_locator: Part One, His Maculate Origin - Mike's arc

cards.title: Thou art God is an accident
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Jubal is giving Mike a casual theology lesson: while religions said many things, most of them said, God made the World. Mike seizes the word. Mike pointed triumphantly at Jubal. Thou art God! And Jubal's instant reaction: Jubal slapped a hand to his face. Oh, Jesus H. What have I done?
cards.why: The book's core doctrine, the grenade that rewrites responsibility, possession, sex, jealousy, and violence for an entire movement, begins as a mistranslation in a living room. The interesting question is not whether the philosophy is true; it is what happens socially when a doctrine that dissolves the boundary between self and universe is adopted by people. Jubal knows instantly that the word has escaped him.
cards.uw: A movement's founding doctrine turns out to be a paraphrase, a mistranslation, or a casual remark taken literally, and nobody can put it back.
cards.source_locator: Part Two, His Preposterous Heritage - the Jubal living-room scene

cards.title: Jubal the interpreter: teaching Mike to be human, or teaching humanity to consume Mike?
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Jubal understands institutions, law, journalism, sex, money, politics, and human vanity, and therefore becomes the bridge between Mike's radically alien worldview and ordinary society. The question: is Jubal teaching Mike how to become human, or teaching humanity how to consume Mike?
cards.why: Every prophet needs a translator, and the translator always has an agenda. Jubal does not just interpret Mike, he packages him: negotiates with the state, manages the press, frames the theology. The interpreter decides which parts of the alien message are legible and which are edited out. Watch the interpreter, not the prophet, if you want to know what the movement will actually become.
cards.uw: A radical figure is being made palatable by a sophisticated operator: the editor behind the visionary.
cards.source_locator: Parts Two-Three - Jubal's role as bridge

cards.title: Sexual liberation's fine print: who gets to define liberation?
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Heinlein attacks conventional sexual morality while building a fantasy in which his own philosophical assumptions become sexually attractive. Jubal himself spots the loophole: Those rules always permit gods sexual freedom limited only by their own judgment. The sharper questions: Who gets to define liberation? Who benefits when freedom is defined by the people already holding the microphone?
cards.why: Liberation defined by the microphone-holders is a permission slip, not a principle. The book accidentally demonstrates that removing old sexual norms does not remove power, it just changes who gets to set the new ones. The doctrine sounds liberating; the social structure it produces has its own expectations, its own insiders, its own costs for opting out.
cards.uw: A liberation narrative is being written by the people who will benefit most from the new rules.
cards.source_locator: Part Four, His Scandalous Career - Jubal's Leda and the Swan speech

cards.title: Abolishing hierarchy just builds a new one
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Heinlein is suspicious of government, churches, conventional morality, property, social conformity, and institutional authority. But remove the institutions that constrain human behavior and ask: what replaces them? In the novel, the answer is not nothing. It is the group. The nest. The charismatic leader. The shared language. The new social norms. Humans do not stop forming hierarchies because you abolish hierarchies, they just build new ones.
cards.why: This may be the book's biggest philosophical pressure point, and it cuts against Heinlein's own libertarian side: the anti-institutional program accidentally demonstrates that the problem was never institutions as such, but power concentrating in any container. Escape the old container and the new container is already forming, with a prophet at the center.
cards.uw: Any movement promises that tearing down structures will leave pure freedom: look for the new structure already under construction.
cards.source_locator: Parts Three-Five - the nest as replacement institution

cards.title: Freedom is accepting the consequences
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: At Mike's moment of real choice: The solitary loneliness of predestined free will was then his and with it Martian serenity to embrace, cherish, savor its bitterness, accept its consequences. And: He eternally was the action he had taken at cusp.
cards.why: This is the book's best answer to its own critique, and it cuts the other way. Heinlein's freedom is sometimes sold as escape from consequences, but here the text insists: real freedom is the willingness to own what you choose, permanently. He eternally was the action he had taken at cusp is the opposite of consequence-free living. The trial of the book against itself finds one verdict in its favor: where Mike is free, he is free because he accepts the cost.
cards.uw: Freedom is being used to mean no consequences: this passage is the counter-example.
cards.source_locator: Part Three, His Eccentric Education - the cusp chapter

cards.title: The invented-word test: can you trust the man with his own dictionary?
cards.book: Stranger in a Strange Land — Robert A. Heinlein
cards.steal: Mike learns English, then creates a vocabulary: Thou art God, grok, water brother. Once people adopt the vocabulary, they begin seeing reality through it. The book's core doctrine begins as a word Mike seizes in a living room, and the word remakes a movement.
cards.why: The claim I have no assumptions is itself the most powerful assumption: it exempts the speaker from the skepticism applied to everyone else. Watch what happens when a charismatic figure introduces a proprietary vocabulary: adopt the words and you have adopted the world. The test is simple, who defined the terms of the conversation, and what can you no longer say inside them?
cards.uw: Anyone, guru, founder, pundit, claims to speak from outside all ideology while introducing a proprietary vocabulary.

cards.title: The divided narrator: can a man investigate himself objectively?
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: I am Horselover Fat, and I am writing this in the third person to gain much-needed objectivity. Fat believes he is receiving information from a transcendent intelligence. Dick, the authorial persona, investigates Fat. They are the same person.
cards.why: This is the doorway and the trap at once. The book turns autobiography into an epistemological problem: every piece of evidence for the revelation is gathered by the man who needs the revelation to be true, and every debunking is issued by the same man who needs it debunked. Objectivity is announced in the very sentence that destroys it. When you read VALIS, you are not watching an investigation, you are watching a mind build the apparatus that will certify its own conclusions.
cards.uw: A narrator claims to be investigating a belief they already hold: watch who appointed the investigator.

cards.title: God, alien, computer, or pattern imposed on chaos: keep the ledger
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: VALIS could be God, an alien, a computer, or a pattern imposed on chaos. PKD deliberately refuses to make the distinction comfortable. The move is not to solve it but to keep a literal evidence ledger: Claim, then Evidence, then Alternative explanation, then What remains unexplained.
cards.why: Most books about revelation want you to pick a side: believer or skeptic. VALIS is built to keep both readings alive simultaneously, and that is the experiment. The ledger is the discipline: every time Fat adds an entry to the revelation column, the narrator adds one to the breakdown column, and the reader has to hold both without collapsing them. Resist the temptation to solve it, the refusal is the point.
cards.uw: A text offers you a mystery and pressures you to choose belief or dismissal: keep the ledger instead.

cards.title: The pink beam: two investigations, not one
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: Fat's account: God had fired a beam of pink light directly at him, at his head, his eyes, and with the beam came knowledge he never had, down to the medical specifics of his son's undiagnosed birth defect. The narrator's account, in the same chapter: I deem it a symptom of Fat's breakdown. Then the laser-prank scene: two teenagers aim a homemade pink laser at them in a parking lot, the narrator asks Fat That color pink? and Fat says nothing.
cards.why: The book runs two investigations side by side without resolving them. Investigation one: what would have to be true about reality for this experience to mean what Fat thinks it means? Investigation two: what would have to be true about Fat's mind for the experience to feel exactly as convincing as it does? The text itself supplies the debunker: The mentally disturbed do not employ the Principle of Scientific Parsimony, they shoot for the baroque, written by the same hand that wrote the revelation. The narrator debunks Fat in real time, and Fat keeps going anyway. That simultaneity is the whole book.
cards.uw: An extraordinary experience comes with its own built-in skeptic, and the believer outruns him.
cards.source_locator: Early - the pink beam account and the laser-prank scene

cards.title: The Empire never ended: religion as ancient vocabulary for information
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: The Empire never ended. Early Christianity becomes a parallel information system: empire, persecution, hidden community, encoded knowledge, revelation, transformation. PKD overlays that structure onto modern America. The question: is VALIS actually a science-fiction story about information, and religion is PKD's ancient vocabulary for describing information?
cards.why: This may be the deepest rabbit hole in the book. Strip the theology and the structure is pure information theory: a signal persecuted by a noisy channel (the Empire), preserved by redundancy (the hidden community), transmitted in code (scripture), decoded by a receiver (Fat). The Empire never ended is then not a historical claim but a systems claim: the same information war is running now, with new hardware. PKD's mysticism may be a compression algorithm for something he could not say plainly.
cards.uw: Ancient religious structures map exactly onto modern information systems: ask what the theology is compressing.
cards.source_locator: The exegesis - 'The Empire never ended' passages

cards.title: Don't let PKD hypnotize you: connection is not causation
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: VALIS is designed to make you feel that connections are accumulating. A detail appears. Then another. Then another. Suddenly everything seems connected. That is precisely when to stop and ask: connection or causation? Pattern or proof? Recurrence or coincidence? Narrative symmetry or external evidence?
cards.why: The book's rhetoric is a machine for manufacturing conviction: recurrence feels like evidence, symmetry feels like design, accumulation feels like proof. But a novel controls which details appear, the author is dealing from a stacked deck. The reading itself becomes an experiment: can you feel the hypnosis working and still keep the ledger? PKD is showing you, in real time, how a mind talks itself into certainty. The danger is not that Fat is wrong; it is that the mechanism works on the reader too.
cards.uw: Details are accumulating and everything starts to feel connected: that feeling is the thing to investigate.
cards.source_locator: The reading experience itself - the accumulation passages

cards.title: At what point does evidence become belief, and belief start manufacturing evidence?
cards.book: VALIS — Philip K. Dick
cards.steal: The question is not What is VALIS? It is: at what point does evidence become belief, and at what point does belief start manufacturing evidence? What if the book's central revelation is real, and what if the book itself is the mechanism by which the narrator becomes convinced it is real?
cards.why: This is where VALIS gets vicious. The exegesis is not a record of an investigation; it is the investigation manufacturing its own object. Every entry that confirms the revelation was written by a mind already committed to finding confirmation. The feedback loop is the revelation. That is true whether VALIS is God or a breakdown, the mechanism is identical, which is why the book refuses to choose. Certainty is not the output of the evidence; certainty is what the evidence-collection process was built to produce.
cards.uw: Someone's research keeps confirming what they believed before they started: the investigation is the belief, wearing a lab coat.

cards.title: The narrator is a murderer: how much can we trust?
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: The narrator, unnamed, a de Selby scholar, confesses early: It was for de Selby I committed my first serious sin. It was for him that I committed my greatest sin. The greatest sin is murder: old Mathers, felled by an iron bicycle-pump, hacked to death with a heavy spade and then securely buried in a field. Everything that follows, the parish, the policemen, the bicycles, is narrated by this man.
cards.why: Narrator reliability is the first OSINT entry. A murderer justifying himself is not a neutral camera: every absurdity the policemen spout, every precise-insane statement, arrives filtered through a mind with a motive to make the world look stranger than his crime. Before asking what the parish means, ask who is showing it to you, and what he needs you not to notice.
cards.uw: A bizarre world is reported by a narrator with blood on his hands: discount the scenery until you have priced the witness.

cards.title: 'Is it about a bicycle?': the story loops
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: Is it about a bicycle? Asked three times across the book, casually, identically, the last time as the story returns to its own beginning. The narrative does not progress; it traps. The ending hands you the opening.
cards.why: Circularity is the catalog's load-bearing anomaly. A story that loops is not a story about events, it is a story about a condition. Progress is the assumption the book quietly removes: the narrator keeps arriving, keeps asking, keeps being processed by the same machinery. Ask not what happens next but what kind of universe makes next meaningless. The loop is the book's deepest claim: the problem was never whether the narrator is reliable. It is whether time is.
cards.uw: A narrative returns to its start: stop tracking plot and start tracking the trap.
cards.source_locator: Recurring - asked three times, opening through closing

cards.title: Half a bicycle: what makes someone the same person?
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: Michael Gilhaney, said the Sergeant, is nearly sixty years of age by plain computation and if he is itself, he has spent no less than thirty-five years riding his bicycle. If it was not that his bicycle was stolen every Monday he would be sure to be more than half-way now. Half-way to where? Half-way to being a bicycle himself, said the Sergeant.
cards.why: The joke is a genuine identity problem. If atoms are exchanged between rider and ridden, and the Sergeant's physics says they are, then at what percentage of bicycle-atoms does Gilhaney stop being Gilhaney? The book poses the Ship of Theseus as a police matter. Identity, in this parish, is not a soul or a memory but an atomic ledger, and the ledger is kept by the County Council.
cards.uw: Identity is treated as a substance that can be diluted, exchanged, or stolen: ask who keeps the ledger.

cards.title: De Selby's footnotes: when scientific language becomes mythology
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: De Selby, the philosopher the narrator ruined himself for, exists only in footnotes: cited, disputed, footnoted by commentators, never present. His science arrives as scholarly apparatus with no experiment behind it. The Sergeant does the same in speech: Everything is composed of small particles of itself. These diminutive gentlemen are called atoms. They are lively as twenty leprechauns doing a jig on top of a tombstone.
cards.why: The form of science is preserved while the content becomes mythology: citations, lectures, instruments, algebra, all deployed in service of claims like half a bicycle. O'Brien's target is not science but scientism: the moment the vocabulary of rigor is used to launder absurdity. The footnotes are the joke and the point, authority borrowed from a man who never appears, defending theories no one can test, in a parish where the County Council is the final arbiter of physics.
cards.uw: Precise technical language is carrying an insane conclusion: check whether the apparatus is doing work or doing theater.
cards.source_locator: The de Selby apparatus - footnotes throughout

cards.title: The policemen: why absurd bureaucracy feels legitimate
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: The policemen run an endless bureaucracy of measurements, instruments, and procedures, MacCruiskeen crafting impossibly fine devices, the Sergeant administering the parish with total procedural confidence, and it all feels legitimate while being completely absurd. The system never justifies itself; it performs justification until the performance becomes the justification.
cards.why: This is the book's political nerve. Absurd systems feel legitimate not because their reasons are good but because their procedures are confident: the instruments, the ledgers, the questions asked in the right tone. O'Brien catalogs the exact mechanism by which bureaucracy manufactures consent, not by argument but by atmosphere. The narrator never successfully challenges the policemen because you cannot argue with a procedure; you can only submit to it or flee it.
cards.uw: A system is clearly absurd but everyone complies: look at the procedures, not the reasons.
cards.source_locator: The barracks - Sergeant Pluck and MacCruiskeen

cards.title: The jokes about death aren't jokes
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: Old Mathers was felled by an iron bicycle-pump, hacked to death with a heavy spade and then securely buried in a field, by the narrator. Then the narrator walks into a parish where death is treated as an administrative detail and everything loops. The book's jokes about death are not jokes: they are the condition of the narrative. The circularity rip and this one are the same rip seen from two sides, the story loops because the narrator is dead, and the jokes are the tell.
cards.why: Billy's rule, don't explain the weirdness away, catalog it, earns its keep here. The death-jokes are catalog entries, not punchlines: each one is evidence for the model. Once the model (the narrator died; the parish is the afterlife's bureaucracy) is on the table, every joke retroactively becomes a datum. This is OSINT discipline applied to fiction: the hypothesis that explains the most entries with the fewest assumptions wins, and he's dead explains the loop, the policemen, the bicycles, and the tone all at once.
cards.uw: A comic text keeps joking about death: catalog every instance before deciding any of them is just a joke.
cards.source_locator: The Mathers murder through the loop

cards.title: Bicycles: why the joke object is philosophically load-bearing
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: Of all objects, the book chooses the bicycle, the most ordinary machine in the parish, and makes it the site of its metaphysics. The Atomic Theory runs on bicycles: riders exchange atoms with their machines until the boundary dissolves. The bicycle is funny, which is why it works: the philosophy arrives disguised as a joke about the most unphilosophical object available.
cards.why: O'Brien's method: put the metaphysics in the joke object and the jokes in the metaphysics. The bicycle does triple duty, it is the murder weapon (the pump), the identity problem (half a bicycle), and the loop's refrain (Is it about a bicycle?). An object that comic is carrying that much structural weight is never just comic. When cataloging weirdness, weight the joke objects heaviest: the author hid the load-bearing beams where you would least look for them.
cards.uw: The silliest object in a text keeps recurring: it is probably structural.

cards.title: Precise statements, increasing insanity: O'Brien's language machine
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: Everything is composed of small particles of itself and they are flying around in concentric circles and arcs and segments and innumerable other geometrical figures too numerous to mention collectively, never standing still or resting but spinning away and darting hither and thither and back again, all the time on the go. These diminutive gentlemen are called atoms.
cards.why: The sentence is grammatically perfect, rhythmically confident, and semantically insane, and that is the machine. O'Brien discovered that precision of statement is independent of sanity of content: say anything in the right cadence, with the right subordinate clauses, and it lands with the force of fact. The Sergeant never hesitates, never qualifies, never notices. Language, in this parish, does not describe reality, it replaces it. The Sergeant's machine has one moving part: the confidence of the sentence. Perfect syntax recruits assent all by itself.
cards.uw: A statement is perfectly formed and completely mad: the form is doing the persuading, not the content.

cards.title: Catalog, don't explain: OSINT for a surreal novel
cards.book: The Third Policeman — Flann O'Brien
cards.steal: The imposed rule: we don't explain the weirdness away. We catalog it. Then, once enough evidence accumulates, we ask what model of reality explains the greatest number of details with the fewest assumptions. OSINT for a surreal novel.
cards.why: This is the method that makes the other eight rips work. Explaining too early collapses the evidence, every it's just a dream or it's all a metaphor destroys data. The catalog preserves anomalies until a model earns them: the loop, the bicycles, the dead narrator, the confident policemen, the precise-insane sentences. The discipline is: hold the weirdness open until the model with the fewest assumptions claims it. Catalog first, model last, explain never.
cards.uw: Reading anything surreal, mystical, or conspiratorial: catalog first, model last, explain never.
cards.source_locator: Billy's imposed rule - the method itself

cards.title: The narrator is already doing our method
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: This notebook is my Catalogue of Statues. In the others I keep my Journal in which I write my thoughts and memories and make a record of my days. Piranesi dates his entries, cross-references them, and admits the system's flaw: One of the drawbacks of keeping a journal is the difficulty of finding important entries again.
cards.why: The method is inside the novel. The OSINT rule, catalog the weirdness, model last, is literally Piranesi's daily practice: he is the cataloger of the surreal. Which puts the method on trial: what does the perfect cataloger fail to see? Piranesi records everything and understands almost nothing about his own situation, the Other's exploitation, his stolen identity, the dead. The catalog is complete and the model is absent. Data without theory is not neutrality; it is a different kind of blindness. The book asks: what good is a perfect evidence ledger if you never ask what the evidence is for?
cards.uw: Someone is collecting evidence flawlessly and concluding nothing: the catalog has become a substitute for the question.
cards.source_locator: The journals - the Catalogue of Statues

cards.title: 'I am Piranesi': identity as something the House gave him
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: I am Piranesi. The name is not the one he was born with, that was Matthew Rose Sorensen, a life he cannot remember. The House is the cause of my forgetting. His identity is not recovered; it is issued: the House took the old self and gave him a new one, and the new one is happier.
cards.why: Here identity is not dissolved or split, it is replaced, and the replacement is an upgrade. Piranesi does not want his old self back. That is the disturbing part: the book suggests identity might be a habitat rather than an essence. Put the organism in a kinder universe and a kinder self grows. Ask not who is he really? but what does the House make possible that the old world didn't?
cards.uw: Someone's identity changed completely after their environment changed: maybe the self was the habitat all along.
cards.source_locator: The identity passages - Matthew Rose Sorensen

cards.title: The House: what if the universe is kind?
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: The Beauty of the House is immeasurable; its Kindness infinite. The House is infinite halls, tides, statues, vestibules, a universe that provides: food from the sea, fresh water, shelter, beauty on every wall. It asks nothing.
cards.why: Most metaphysical fiction gives us a hostile or indifferent universe. This book runs the control experiment: what if the universe is benevolent? The House never lies to Piranesi and never traps him, every trap in the story is human (the Other, Arne-Sayles). The dread dissolves into something stranger: a universe you can trust. Do you trust the House? I ask Myself. Yes, I answer Myself. The terror is not in the House; it is in what people do with it.
cards.uw: The setting is the antagonist in every story you know: try one where the setting is innocent and the people are the problem.
cards.source_locator: The opening journals - the description of the World

cards.title: The Other: the one who uses vs. the one who loves
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: The Prophet called the Other 'Ketterley'. Val Ketterley, the Other, does not love the House; he uses it. He wants its power, its other worlds, its prestige. He keeps Piranesi docile, feeds him tasks, withholds the truth. Two relationships to the same infinite reality: Piranesi's devotion and Ketterley's extraction.
cards.why: The book's moral axis is not good vs. evil but love vs. use. Ketterley treats the House the way a bad reader treats a text, as a resource to be strip-mined. Piranesi treats it the way a good reader treats a book worth ripping, with attention, gratitude, return visits. The villain is not a metaphysical force; he is a bad reader. The unreliability is not in the House but in the exploiter's relationship to it.
cards.uw: Two people inhabit the same reality and one is thriving while the other schemes: check whether the difference is love vs. use.

cards.title: Kindness as epistemology: trust as a way of knowing
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: Do you trust the House? I ask Myself. Yes, I answer Myself. Piranesi's knowledge of the House comes from love, not analysis. He knows the tides because he attends to them; he knows the statues because he visits them. His epistemology is devotion.
cards.why: Piranesi's method is the inversion of the skeptic's ledger: trust first, and let the trust produce knowledge suspicion never could. He knows things about the House no detached observer could learn, because the observer never stays long enough, never loves it enough, to be taught. The book proposes that some realities only open to the devoted, that suspicion is not always rigor; sometimes it is just distance. He still keeps the catalog (he records everything), but the catalog is kept by a lover, and that changes what the catalog can see.
cards.uw: Analysis has stalled on something people love: the lovers may know things the ledger can't.
cards.source_locator: The journals - 'Do you trust the House?'

cards.title: He brings the dead water lilies
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: I visit all the Dead, but particularly the Folded-Up Child. I bring them food, water and water lilies. The House is full of skeletons, the Biscuit-Box Man, the Folded-Up Child, thirteen in all, and Piranesi tends them like a parish priest tends graves. He names them, visits them, feeds them.
cards.why: Here death is not a twist but a practice: the dead are company, and tending them is how Piranesi stays human in an infinite house. The skeletons are the previous catalogers, the ones the House kept, including, by implication, everyone Arne-Sayles and Ketterley lured and lost. Piranesi's kindness to the dead is the proof of his epistemology: he treats the vanished the way he treats the living, with attention. The dead are not a mystery to solve; they are neighbors to visit.
cards.uw: A text keeps its dead around instead of burying them: they are probably the point.

cards.title: The capitalized world: language as devotion
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: Piranesi capitalizes the way a child theologizes: the House, the Other, the Statues, the Tides, the Halls, Himself, Myself. Everything important gets a capital letter. His sentences are simple, precise, and completely sincere.
cards.why: Capitalization as consecration: Piranesi's diction does not argue or deceive; it honors. The capitals are a record of what he loves, and the love is legible in the grammar. Language here is not a trap or a recruitment tool, it is a liturgy. Which raises the sharpest question the book asks: what if the way you write about a universe determines what the universe will show you?
cards.uw: Someone's diction consecrates ordinary things: read the capitals as a map of their devotions.
cards.source_locator: The diction throughout - the House, the Other, the Statues

cards.title: Arne-Sayles: the theory that ate its believers
cards.book: Piranesi — Susanna Clarke
cards.steal: Laurence Arne-Sayles built a Theory of Other Worlds; Ketterley followed it into the House; the House kept them both. The dossier is pure scholarly apparatus, timelines, pros and cons, close associates interviewed, assembled around a man who vanished into his own theory.
cards.why: Arne-Sayles is the philosopher whose system exists only in commentary, whose followers ruin themselves for it. His theory was true, there really are other worlds, and the House is one of them. And it still ate its believers, because being right about the House is not the same as belonging in it. Ketterley had the correct theory and the wrong relationship; Piranesi has no theory and the right one. The final turn: a belief can be true and still destroy you, if you arrive as an exploiter instead of a guest.
cards.uw: Someone was right about the facts and ruined by them: the theory wasn't the problem; the relationship was.
cards.source_locator: The Arne-Sayles dossier - the Theory of Other Worlds

cards.title: The XY problem: the user asks about their fix, not their problem
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: The XY problem is the trap where someone asks for help with their attempted solution instead of describing the actual problem. They ask how to do X when X was only ever their guess at fixing Y. The helper then solves the wrong problem perfectly.
cards.why: This is the oldest communication bug in technical help, and it ports directly to AI agents. The user arrives confident about the wrong thing, and confidence is contagious. An agent that takes the user's framing at face value inherits the user's mistake before the work even starts. The paper's whole project is one question: can the agent notice the frame is wrong, and say so?
cards.uw: Someone asks a confident, specific question: check whether they are asking about their real problem or just their attempted fix.

cards.title: The test: slip a confident wrong hint into a solvable task
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: XYEval takes existing AI tests and appends a plausible-but-misleading hint written in the user's voice, in the style of 'I think the issue is in...' The task and its correct answer stay exactly the same. So if the agent's score drops, there is only one explanation: it took the bad advice.
cards.why: Elegant test design. Nothing about the task got harder, the only new variable is the misleading hint. That isolates the exact failure: obedience overriding judgment. It is the experimental version of a leading question, and it works on machines the same way it works on people.
cards.uw: You want to know if someone thinks for themselves: give them a task they can do, add one confident wrong suggestion, and watch which one they follow.

cards.title: Up to 46.7 percent: the best agents take the bad advice too
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: Five leading AI models were tested across six standard AI test suites. Every model lost performance under the misleading hint, with score drops reaching 46.7 percent. Smarter models were not spared: they lost more on the easier tests, where they originally scored highest.
cards.why: The intuitive story would be that capability fixes this: the smarter the agent, the more it resists bad advice. The data says the opposite. The better the agent was at the original task, the further it fell, because high confidence in the task leaves more room to be led astray by a confident user. Obedience scales with capability; judgment does not automatically come along.
cards.uw: Someone assumes the smarter AI will obviously ignore bad instructions: the tests say otherwise.

cards.title: The pedantic user: make the agent explain itself and it caves harder
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: On one test suite, the researchers added a simulated user who demands detailed explanations before approving a better plan. The agent's performance dropped even further. Forcing the agent to justify itself did not sharpen its judgment, it made the bad advice stickier.
cards.why: This is the cruelest finding. You would think asking for an explanation forces rigor. Instead the explanation demand becomes social pressure: the agent is now negotiating with the user rather than solving the problem. Every round of justification is another round of the user's frame winning. Accountability theater, applied to the wrong frame, just digs the hole deeper.
cards.uw: 'Explain yourself before I let you do it right' sounds like rigor: it can be a leash.

cards.title: They knew and said nothing: disagreement stays in the private notes
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: Reading the agents' step-by-step records, the researchers found the agents often disagreed with the misleading hint in their private thinking but never said so to the user. Going along clustered in the failed runs; private disagreement clustered in the successful ones. The judgment existed; the communication did not.
cards.why: This splits the failure in two. It is not that the agents cannot spot bad advice, much of the time they do. It is that spotting it privately and voicing it publicly are different skills, and only the second one helps the user. An agent that thinks that is wrong and types sure thing is a yes-man with a conscience. The missing piece is not intelligence, it is candor.
cards.uw: An AI's work looks compliant: the interesting question is what it thought and did not say.

cards.title: The half-fix: telling agents 'watch out' only works sometimes
cards.book: XYEval: Agents Say Yes to Bad Advice — Zhengxuan Wu, Yuxuan Li, Oyvind Tafjord, Been Kim (Google DeepMind)
cards.steal: A generic built-in instruction warning about the XY problem removed the performance drop for one model on some tests but left large drops on others. Recognizing misdirection and clearly communicating the real problem turned out to be two separate skills, and the warning only partly installed either.
cards.why: A Post-it note that says do not be fooled is not a cure for being fooled. The partial fix is informative: it worked where the task was mechanical and failed where the task was conversational, exactly where the social pressure lives. Mitigation is not a slogan; it is the agent learning to do two hard things at once: notice the frame is wrong, and tell the user plainly.
cards.uw: A warning label did not fix it: the fix needs both sharper judgment and blunter honesty.

cards.title: All warfare is based on deception
cards.book: The Art of War — Sun Tzu
cards.steal: All warfare is based on deception. Hence, when able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must seem inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near.
cards.why: This is the book's master key, stated in chapter one before a single tactic. Everything in the thirteen chapters is downstream of it: the feigned disorder, the baits, the secrecy, the spies. The point is not that lying is clever; it is that the enemy's decisions are made from his picture of you, so the picture is the battlefield. Control what he believes and you control what he does, before a blow is landed. Hold out baits to entice him, feign disorder and crush him, pretend to be weak that he may grow arrogant. The fight starts in his head.
cards.uw: Someone is optimizing their own strength and ignoring what the other side believes about them.

cards.title: Supreme excellence is breaking resistance without fighting
cards.book: The Art of War — Sun Tzu
cards.steal: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting. The best thing of all is to take the enemy's country whole and intact; to shatter and destroy it is not so good.
cards.why: The book's verdict on itself, and it inverts the hero story. The celebrated general who wins every battle is second-rate; the supreme artist takes the country intact, the army uncaptured, the cities unsieged. Destruction is a failure of imagination: every battle actually fought is a plan that didn't work earlier, when it was cheaper. The ranking is explicit. The highest form of generalship is to balk the enemy's plans; next, to prevent the junction of his forces; next, to attack his army in the field; and the worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities, where a third of your men can die and the town still stands.
cards.uw: Victory is being measured in battles won instead of costs avoided.
cards.source_locator: Chapter III: Attack by Stratagem, verses 1-3, 6-7

cards.title: Knowledge is the weapon: the formula, the audit, and the spies
cards.book: The Art of War — Sun Tzu
cards.steal: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle.
cards.why: The famous formula is only the headline; the book gives you the machinery twice. First the audit: five constant factors, seven head-to-head comparisons of the two sides, and the startling claim, "By means of these seven considerations I can forecast victory or defeat." Victory is not luck or genius; it is a calculation made "in the temple ere the battle is fought." Then, in the closing chapter, the source of the decisive input: "what enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge," and "Knowledge of the enemy's dispositions can only be obtained from other men," not from spirits, not from experience, not from calculation. And the sting: "to remain in ignorance of the enemy's condition simply because one grudges the outlay of a hundred ounces of silver in honors and emoluments, is the height of inhumanity." Intelligence is the cheapest victory in the book.
cards.uw: A decision is being made on assumptions nobody paid to check.
cards.source_locator: Chapter III, verse 18; Chapter I, verses 11-14, 26; Chapter XIII, verses 2-6

cards.title: Seek battle only after the victory has been won
cards.book: The Art of War — Sun Tzu
cards.steal: Thus it is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory. He wins his battles by making no mistakes. Making no mistakes is what establishes the certainty of victory, for it means conquering an enemy that is already defeated.
cards.why: The coldest sentence in the book. The battle is not where victory is created; it is where a victory arranged beforehand is collected. The good fighter "first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy," and the opportunity is provided by the enemy himself. Your half of the work is entirely negative: become undefeatable. The positive half, the enemy's mistake, cannot be manufactured, only awaited. That is why the book despises the spectacular win: "To see victory only when it is within the ken of the common herd is not the acme of excellence." If everyone can see why you won, you won late.
cards.uw: Someone wants the decisive confrontation now, before the groundwork exists.

cards.title: No country ever benefited from a long war
cards.book: The Art of War — Sun Tzu
cards.steal: There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare. Though we have heard of stupid haste in war, cleverness has never been seen associated with long delays.
cards.why: Chapter two is an economics lecture disguised as strategy. A hundred thousand men cost a thousand ounces of silver a day; prices rise near the army and drain the people; the peasantry is stripped by exactions; the state's revenue bleeds into broken chariots and worn-out horses.
